content_blocks.title: Core idea

Publishing is a supply-chain boundary. Make versions traceable to source commits, authenticate with scoped credentials, record provenance where supported, and validate artifacts before promotion. content_blocks.code:
name: Publish a package
on:
  release:
    types: [published]
permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write
jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Replace with package build and registry login
        run: echo "Build and publish only after validation"
content_blocks.expected_output: A published release starts a job with package-write permission; the example leaves registry-specific build and publication commands as an explicit integration step.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Test packaging separately and grant `packages: write` only to a job that must publish.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove write permission from validation jobs and test authentication in a non-production package.

troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
